name: Thymalin

lead: Thymalin is a calf-thymus extract developed in Russia as an immune-modulating drug and promoted within the Khavinson family of bioregulator peptides for ageing. Looksmaxxing interest is a general hope that a healthier immune system supports ageing well.

The chain runs from thymic peptides to immune modulation to a healthier ageing profile. Proponents say its peptides support T-cell differentiation; the dipeptide Thymogen and the synthetic Vilon were derived from it. Support comes mostly from animal studies and reports by its developers.

paras: It is used in periodic courses, usually in Russian-style bioregulator protocols or alongside other longevity peptides. Users generally expect general, gradual effects rather than a visible change.
The sources reviewed do not describe human adverse effects. It is an animal-derived preparation, and legal status varies by country.

angle.text: Thymalin is a calf-thymus extract used in Russia as an immune drug and taken by longevity enthusiasts hoping for healthier ageing. Data comes mostly from its developers; appearance outcomes have not been measured.

lead: Thymalin is a Russian pharmaceutical preparation made by mild acid extraction of calf thymus. It was put into practice there as an immunocorrector, a drug meant to modulate immune function.[1]

In peptide and anti-aging circles it is discussed as a thymic bioregulator: a short-chain peptide complex said to restore the declining thymus and, through immune and whole-body effects, to slow signs of ageing. People interested in looking younger sometimes include it alongside Epithalamin or Epitalon in so-called Khavinson peptide protocols.[2][3]

From the extract the same research group isolated the dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp, later sold as Thymogen, and designed the synthetic dipeptide Vilon.[1][4] Evidence is mainly from animal and cell studies plus clinical reports from the developing group; no randomized trial of Thymalin for appearance has been published.
infobox: Prescription-type drug in Russia; research peptide elsewhere

paras: Natural thymic peptides were isolated from calf thymus by mild acid extraction, and a pharmaceutical containing them was named Thymalin.[1] The extract is a complex mixture and the group has also studied purified or synthetic components.[1][4]

Thymalin comes from the Saint Petersburg research school of Vladimir Khavinson, whose peptide bioregulators have been described since 1973 and are marketed as Khavinson Peptides.[5] Thymalin was the thymus-derived member of the series; the pineal-derived counterpart is Epithalamin, and later short synthetic peptides such as Epitalon, Vilon and Thymogen followed.[5][2] A similar line of calf thymus extracts exists in Poland: a semipurified extract called TFX has been produced there by the state pharmaceutical industry since 1973 and was evaluated in over 1,000 patients with immune-related conditions, according to a 1989 review.[6]

Vladimir Khavinson (1946 to 2024), the gerontologist most associated with Thymalin, directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and headed the gerontology and geriatrics chair at North-Western State Medical University. Wikipedia credits him with extracting more than 20 peptide complexes from organs and synthesizing about 15 others, with patents in many countries, and lists Thymalin as a thymus preparation described as a regulator of cellular immunity.[7] The same article says six peptide preparations were permitted for medical use in the USSR, Russia and later CIS countries, mainly in military medical service, and it does not describe approval by Western regulators; it also notes that most cited sources are by Khavinson or collaborators and that safety statements rest on his own studies and books.[7]

A 1997 review by the group describes the pathway from the natural thymic complex to Thymogen (the dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp) and the synthetic dipeptide Vilon, positioning Thymalin as the starting point of a family of immunocorrector drugs.[1] A 2002 overview of the group's peptide work states that of the effects of Thymalin the ability to stimulate immunity is the most prominent, and that this is associated with anticarcinogenic and geroprotector activities in the authors' account.[2]

Reviews from the developing group state that Thymalin and related peptides modulate immunity, and that a thymic peptide plus a pineal peptide prolonged life in older people in a long-term study.[3] The dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp derived from Thymalin is reported to have slowed ageing and inhibited spontaneous tumours in rats.[4] A 2018 paper examined Thymalin's effect on tumour and thymus under activation therapy in vivo.[8] A 2022 cell study included Thymalin among five peptides tested in THP-1 monocyte/macrophage cells.[5] An older mouse study examined thymic preparations in experimental parasite infection.[9]

A 2010 review of the thymus-pineal relationship in ageing summarised data that pineal peptides (Epithalamin, Epitalon) were more effective at counteracting thymus involution than thymic peptides (Thymalin, Thymogen) were at counteracting pineal involution.[10] A 2020 paper from the same group reported that Thymalin activated differentiation of human hematopoietic stem cells in culture.[11]

The developing group proposes that thymic peptides help restore thymus function, which declines with age, and so support T-cell differentiation and wider homeostasis.[2][10] For the derived dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp, the authors report activation of T-cell differentiation, changes in intracellular cyclic nucleotides and activation of neutrophil chemotaxis in experimental systems.[4] A 2020 study from the group reported that Thymalin activated differentiation of human hematopoietic stem cells in culture,[11] and a 2022 study tested it among peptides affecting proliferation and inflammatory pathways in monocyte/macrophage THP-1 cells.[5] These are laboratory findings, and the mechanism in people has not been established by independent work.

Clinical reports come mainly from the Russian and Ukrainian groups that developed the drug. The best known is a study by researchers at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and a Kiev institute that followed 266 elderly and older people for 6 to 8 years, with Thymalin or Epithalamin applied during the first 2 to 3 years.[3][12] The authors reported improved cardiovascular, endocrine, immune and nervous system indices, a 2.0 to 2.4-fold lower incidence of acute respiratory disease compared with controls, and about a 2.0 to 2.1-fold lower mortality in the Thymalin-treated group during follow-up.[12] These are reports from the developers rather than independent replications.

In the 266-person study, bioregulators were given during the first two to three years of a six-to-eight-year observation period. The authors reported reduced incidence of ischemic heart disease manifestations, hypertension, deforming osteoarthrosis and osteoporosis compared with controls, alongside the lower respiratory-disease incidence and a 2.0 to 2.1-fold lower mortality among Thymalin-treated patients; an English-language report of the work carries the title 'Peptides of pineal gland and thymus prolong human life'.[3][12]

Other controlled reports in Eastern European journals include a Polish trial in 208 patients with multiple myeloma comparing chemotherapy regimens and immunomodulating treatment,[13] a controlled study of prevention of postoperative complications in diffuse purulent peritonitis in children,[14] and the combined-treatment reports listed below. These studies are small and, as the abstracts describe them, concern hospital conditions rather than cosmetic outcomes.

Other reports from Ukrainian and Russian journals describe Thymalin as part of combined treatment in conditions including parkinsonism (1999), non-specific ulcerative colitis (1992), acute necrotic pancreatitis (2004) and chronic inflammation of the female reproductive organs, where a 2015 comparison with another immunomodulator examined time-of-day effects on lymphocyte response.[15][16][17][18] None of these evaluated skin, hair or facial appearance.
A 1997 review describes use as an immunocorrector in practice.[1]

Thymalin appears in discussions of Khavinson-style peptide bioregulator regimens, where it is sometimes grouped with Epithalamin and Epitalon as part of a rotating set of short courses, and proponents describe the aim as slowing physiological ageing. The research base cited by proponents is the developing group's own animal studies and the 266-person observational follow-up.[2][3][12] People hoping for a younger-looking appearance reason along the chain of immune and organ health leading to visible ageing; no study has measured skin, hair or facial appearance.[3][12]
